```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(pdmS7)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  error = FALSE, collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8,
  fig.height = 3.6, dpi = if (nzchar(Sys.getenv("IN_PKGDOWN"))) 110 else 60
)
pal <- c("#444444", "#236b83", "#a26421", "#5b8c3a", "#8a3b6b", "#b23b3b", "#9aa7b0")
f0 <- function(x) sprintf("%.0f", x)
f2 <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)
```

A synthetic river is a calibration problem whose answer is known. Rain from a stochastic
generator drives a PDM with chosen parameters, and a simulated gauge records the flow with
the faults real gauges have. Calibrate to it and you can see, parameter by parameter, what a
method recovers and what it cannot. It needs no data, so it is also the quickest way to try
the whole package.

Two functions do the work:

- `synthetic_rain()` generates rain and potential evaporation at any step from 15 minutes to a
  day, by one of four methods, from built-in parameters or parameters fitted to a real gauge.
- `synthetic_catchment()` drives the PDM with that rain and adds storms, gauge error and an
  extrapolated rating.

# Rain

## Four generators

| Method | How it makes rain | Steps | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|
| `nsrp` (default) | Neyman-Scott rectangular pulses: storms arrive at random, each spawning rain cells with their own delay, duration and intensity | Any | Sub-daily rain with realistic storms |
| `bartlett_lewis` | Bartlett-Lewis rectangular pulses: a storm produces cells at a steady rate until it stops | Any | The same, by the other classic model |
| `markov_gamma` | Wet and dry days from a Markov chain, amounts from a gamma distribution | Daily | Simple daily rain |
| `resample` | Blocks of whole days drawn from a real record, from the same time of year | The record's | Rain exactly like the gauge's, in a new order |

All four change with the seasons: their parameters are set month by month. The built-in
parameters are illustrative, chosen to resemble lowland England (about 760 mm a year, gentle
frontal rain in winter, short intense storms in summer), and fitted to no particular site.
All three parametric generators describe the same climate.

```{r generators}
gen <- function(method, dt) {
  synthetic_rain("2000-10-01", years = 30, dt = dt, method = method, seed = 1)
}
daily <- list(nsrp = gen("nsrp", 24), bartlett_lewis = gen("bartlett_lewis", 24),
              markov_gamma = gen("markov_gamma", 24))
summary_of <- function(r) {
  wet <- r$rain > 0.1
  c(mm_per_year = sum(r$rain) / 30, wet_days = mean(wet), mean_wet_day_mm = mean(r$rain[wet]),
    wettest_day_mm = max(r$rain))
}
round(sapply(daily, summary_of), 2)
```

The three agree on the totals and the share of wet days. They differ in the extremes, which is
where the models differ most: the pulse models build heavy days from overlapping cells, the
Markov chain from the tail of one gamma distribution.

```{r seasons, fig.height=3.4}
monthly <- sapply(daily, function(r) tapply(r$rain, as.POSIXlt(r$time)$mon, sum) / 30)
matplot(1:12, monthly, type = "l", lty = 1, lwd = 2, col = pal[2:4], xaxt = "n",
        xlab = "", ylab = "Mean rain (mm a month)")
axis(1, 1:12, month.abb)
legend("bottomleft", colnames(monthly), col = pal[2:4], lwd = 2, bty = "n")
```

## Statistics the pulse models reproduce exactly

For the two pulse models, the mean, variance, lag-1 autocorrelation and proportion of dry
intervals have exact formulas at any interval length. `rain_statistics()` computes them, and
for a record it computes the same statistics from the data. The model's figures and those of a
30-year simulation agree to within the scatter of a 30-year sample:

```{r exact}
hourly <- synthetic_rain("2000-10-01", years = 30, dt = 1, seed = 2, pet = NULL)
model <- rain_statistics(rain_parameters("nsrp"), hours = c(1, 24))
data <- rain_statistics(hourly, hours = c(1, 24))
january <- rbind(model = model[model$month == 1, -1], simulated = data[data$month == 1, -1])
round(january[order(january$hours), ], 3)
```

## Fitting to a real gauge

`fit_rain()` fits any of the three parametric generators to a record, month by month. The
pulse models are fitted by matching those statistics at 1 and 24 hours (24 and 72 hours for a
daily record); the Markov chain by maximum likelihood. A record read with reach.io can be passed
straight in:

```{r reach-io, eval=FALSE}
gauge <- reach.io::read_silver("data/hydrometric", "SS92F014", "P", start = "1995-01-01")
parameters <- fit_rain(gauge, "nsrp")
rain <- synthetic_rain("2030-10-01", years = 50, parameters = parameters)
# Or keep the gauge's own rain, in a new order:
rain <- synthetic_rain("2030-10-01", years = 50, method = "resample", record = gauge)
```

Without a real gauge to hand, the hourly series above stands in for one. Fitting the
Neyman-Scott model to it recovers its statistics:

```{r fit}
fitted <- fit_rain(hourly, "nsrp")
check <- attr(fitted, "fit")
round(check[check$month %in% c(1, 7), c("month", "hours", "variance_record", "variance_model",
                                        "pdry_record", "pdry_model")], 3)
```

```{r fit-error, include=FALSE}
var_err <- 100 * max(abs(check$variance_model / check$variance_record - 1))
pdry_err <- max(abs(check$pdry_model - check$pdry_record))
```

Across all twelve months, the fitted variances are within `r f0(var_err)` per cent of the
record's and the dry proportions within `r f2(pdry_err)`. The parameters themselves are less
well determined than the statistics: several combinations of storm rate, cells per storm and
cell size give much the same rain. That is a property of the model, not of the fit, and it
does no harm when the aim is realistic rain.

# The river

`synthetic_catchment()` takes the rain (generating it if none is given), adds any storms you
name, runs a PDM, and records the flow through a simulated gauge.

```{r river}
river <- synthetic_catchment(
  years = 10, dt = 24, area_km2 = 60, seed = 4,
  storms = data.frame(time = "2016-01-05", depth_mm = 150, duration_h = 48),
  error = list(sd = 0.05, memory_h = 72),
  highest_gauged_m3s = 10
)
river
```

| Part | What it does |
|---|---|
| True model | The standard structure with a lowland water balance: soil capacity up to 300 mm, slow drainage to groundwater above a 50 mm threshold, surface stores of 12 hours. Every calibrated parameter lies inside `calibration_bounds()`, so a calibration can in principle recover it. Pass `truth` to use any configuration |
| Start | Spun up over the first year, so the record starts in balance |
| Storms | Each adds a depth over a duration, in a triangular profile. They guarantee floods larger than ten years of generated rain would give |
| Gauge error | Multiplicative and persistent: an AR(1) process in logs, here with a 5 per cent standard deviation and a three-day memory. Real gauge errors drift; they do not flicker |
| Rating | Exact up to the highest gauged flow, then bent low, as an extrapolated rating often is |

```{r river-plot, fig.height=3.8}
rows <- which(river$forcing$time >= as.POSIXct("2015-12-01", tz = "UTC"))[1:90]
time <- river$forcing$time[rows]
plot(time, river$true_flow[rows], type = "l", col = pal[3], lwd = 1.5, lty = 2, xlab = "",
     ylab = "Flow (m3/s)", ylim = c(0, max(river$true_flow[rows]) * 1.05))
points(time, river$observed[rows], pch = 16, cex = 0.5, col = pal[1])
abline(h = river$highest_gauged_m3s, lty = 2, col = pal[7])
legend("topright", c("true flow", "recorded", "highest gauging"), col = pal[c(3, 1, 7)],
       lty = c(2, NA, 2), pch = c(NA, 16, NA), bty = "n")
```

```{r rating, include=FALSE}
peak <- which.max(river$true_flow)
under <- 100 * (1 - river$observed[peak] / river$true_flow[peak])
```

At the storm's peak the gauge records `r f0(river$observed[peak])` m3/s against a true
`r f0(river$true_flow[peak])`: `r f0(under)` per cent low, mostly from the rating.

# Calibrating to it

The river drops straight into the rest of the package. Here, the standard preset is
calibrated to the first six years and checked on the rest:

```{r calibrate}
start <- pdm_presets("standard")
start$dt <- 24
start$area_km2 <- 60
bounds <- calibration_bounds(start)
f <- river$forcing
cal <- f$time < as.POSIXct("2016-10-01", tz = "UTC")
fit <- calibrate_pdm(start, f[cal, ], river$observed[cal],
                     lower = setNames(bounds$lower, bounds$path),
                     upper = setNames(bounds$upper, bounds$path),
                     log_scale = bounds$path[bounds$scale == "log"], warmup = 90,
                     objective = "nse", starts = 3, seed = 1, control = list(maxit = 40))
compare <- data.frame(
  truth = sapply(bounds$path, function(p) pdmS7:::.path_get(river$truth, p)),
  calibrated = signif(fit$parameters, 3)
)
compare
model <- pdm_from_config(fit$config)
sim <- run_pdm(model, f[c("rain", "pet")],
               initial_state_from_flow(model, river$observed[1], 0.7))$output$q_m3s
later <- !cal
c(nse_against_recorded = pdm_scorecard(sim[later], river$observed[later])[["nse"]],
  nse_against_truth = pdm_scorecard(sim[later], river$true_flow[later])[["nse"]])
```

```{r equifinal, include=FALSE}
kb_ratio <- fit$parameters[["groundwater.kb"]] / river$truth$groundwater$kb
```

The calibrated parameters are not the true ones: `kb` is `r f0(kb_ratio)` times too large, and
the two surface stores, both 12 hours in truth, come out at
`r f0(fit$parameters[["surface.k1"]])` and `r f0(fit$parameters[["surface.k2"]])` hours. Yet the fit scores
`r f2(pdm_scorecard(sim[later], river$true_flow[later])[["nse"]])` against the truth. Many
parameter sets fit a record almost equally well; [Larger floods](extrapolation.html) shows
where that matters.

Only on a synthetic river can the last line be computed: the score against the truth, rather
than against a gauge that has its own errors.

# What else to try

| Question | How |
|---|---|
| What does structural error do? | Pass a different `truth`, such as a split recharge or an exponential store from `structure_set()`, and calibrate the standard structure to it |
| Does a calibration extrapolate? | Register the river in a calibration project; the wettest years are held back and tested. See [Larger floods](extrapolation.html) |
| How do forecasts degrade with lead time? | Use the river in a hindcast with `pdm_hindcast()`. See [Hindcasts](hindcasts.html) |
| What does a 15-minute record change? | `synthetic_rain(dt = 0.25)` and a `truth` with `dt = 0.25` |
| How much do gauge errors matter? | Vary `error`, `highest_gauged_m3s` and `rating_bias`, and compare the scores against the truth |

# Limits

A synthetic river flatters every method run on it. The true model is a PDM, the rain is known
exactly, and the gauge's errors follow a simple rule. Use it to understand methods and to test
code, not to predict how well a calibration will do on a real catchment.

# References

Cowpertwait, P.S.P. (1996) Further developments of the Neyman-Scott clustered point process
for modeling rainfall. *Water Resources Research* 32(7), 2155-2164.

Richardson, C.W. (1981) Stochastic simulation of daily precipitation, temperature, and solar
radiation. *Water Resources Research* 17(1), 182-190.

Rodriguez-Iturbe, I., Cox, D.R. and Isham, V. (1987) Some models for rainfall based on
stochastic point processes. *Proceedings of the Royal Society of London A* 410, 269-288.
